DStv is fighting pirates
with serious technology.
Here's why people became pirates.

Canal+ — DStv's new French owner — has deployed forensic watermarking, ISP blocking, and just won a court ruling in France that forces Google, Cloudflare, and Cisco to block pirate streams. The technology is genuinely impressive. So is the question it leaves unanswered: why did millions of South Africans become pirates in the first place?

Jarrit Hosking
Forge Vertical · Cape Town · August 29, 2026
10 min read
// Chapter 01 — The technology first

Give Canal+ credit for this: they are not fighting piracy with press releases. They are fighting it with technology that is genuinely sophisticated, and the results are starting to show.

(cite index="20-1">DStv's cybersecurity company Irdeto uses IP blocking and forensic watermarking to fight content piracy. "Illegal streaming services, illicit IPTV platforms, pirate websites, and unauthorised content distribution have evolved into a sophisticated digital ecosystem," the company said. "Content can be copied, repackaged, and redistributed almost instantly, often across multiple platforms and jurisdictions."

(cite index="19-1">Canal+ employs advanced technology including ISP blocking and forensic watermarking as key tools in disrupting sophisticated piracy operations. Recent raids resulted in the deactivation of 819 pirate streaming accounts and arrests under the Cybercrimes Act.

The watermarking is the most interesting part. (cite index="20-1">DStv content includes forensic watermarks — invisible identifiers — that enable Irdeto to determine where pirated content originated. "If that content later appears on an illegal service, the watermark can help identify where the content came from and, in some applications, the individual stream or account involved," the company said. "Irdeto's TraceMark technology is designed to maintain this traceability even when content has been re-encoded, resized, captured, or otherwise manipulated."

This is not trivial. Forensic watermarking that survives re-encoding and screen capture is a genuinely difficult technical problem. The piracy ecosystem has adapted to remove obvious watermarks for years. Invisible, manipulation-resistant watermarks that can trace a stream back to a specific account — even after it has been repackaged and redistributed — represent a meaningful step forward in the technical arms race between rights holders and pirates.

// Canal+ / Irdeto anti-piracy technology stack

// 01 — Forensic watermarking
TraceMark — invisible identifiers that survive re-encoding
Invisible markers embedded in every DStv stream at the account level. If pirated content appears on an illegal service, the watermark identifies which account the content originated from — even after re-encoding, resizing, screen capture, or format conversion. Creates a direct chain between detection and enforcement.
// 02 — ISP blocking
Direct blocking of pirate stream sources at internet service provider level
Rather than chasing individual users — impractical at scale — Irdeto targets the upstream providers in foreign countries that manage illegal streaming services. ISP-level blocking cuts access to the source rather than playing whack-a-mole with individual subscribers.
// 03 — DNS blocking via court order
Paris court ruling forces Google, Cloudflare, and Cisco to block pirate streams
(cite index="21-1">A new court ruling in France — the Paris Court of Appeal — ruled in favour of Canal+ for the blocking of illegal streaming and IPTV services by alternative DNS providers including Google, Cloudflare, and Cisco. Canal+ described this as a "first-of-its-kind decision" and a "decisive turning point." Canal+ plans to reinforce this across its markets including South Africa.
// 04 — Management panel infiltration
Gaining access to pirate operators' own systems
(cite index="19-1">Authorities gained access to a pirate streaming provider's management panel through Irdeto and identified 715 active accounts. Following deactivation, all 715 users were immediately unable to access their streams. The main reseller was arrested. This approach — targeting the operator infrastructure rather than individual subscribers — is significantly more efficient than trying to pursue end users.

Now the harder question

// Chapter 02 — Why people became pirates

The technology is effective. The arrests are real. The court rulings are significant. And none of it addresses the underlying question: why did millions of South Africans turn to illegal streaming in the first place?

The answer is not primarily that South Africans are dishonest. It is that the legal options failed them, and in some cases, the rights holders themselves drove them away.

"Canal+, MultiChoice, and M-Net actively driving people who are DStv subscribers to piracy, because that content used to be on M-Net and packages like DStv Premium." — Industry source, MyBroadband, 2026

(cite index="18-1">Canal+ is now, ironically, driving DStv customers to piracy — because content that used to be on M-Net and DStv Premium packages has been removed and placed behind Canal+ exclusivity. The content subscribers paid for, sometimes for years, is no longer available on the packages they paid for. The response of a rational consumer is to find that content elsewhere. The illegal streaming services are ready and waiting.

(cite index="24-1">The rise of Netflix initially saw many people move away from online piracy as Netflix solved their problem. However, the fragmentation of content across multiple streaming platforms caused many people to return to online piracy. Online video-on-demand content was centralised through Netflix — and then the studios pulled their content back to launch their own services.

This is the pattern across the global streaming industry, and South Africa is not immune to it. The consumer is being asked to maintain multiple expensive subscriptions to access content that used to be available in one place, at a price point that many South African households cannot sustain. (cite index="24-1">Axxess, one of South Africa's largest ISPs, has reported a 20% increase in torrent activity in recent months. People are not becoming pirates because enforcement has weakened. They are becoming pirates because the legitimate alternatives are too fragmented and too expensive.

The Canal+ paradox

// Chapter 03 — The new owner's challenge

Canal+ acquired MultiChoice in December 2025 and immediately inherited two contradictory pressures. On one side: a piracy problem that costs the business real revenue and requires sustained, expensive technical enforcement. On the other: a pricing and content strategy that is actively creating the conditions for piracy to grow.

(cite index="22-1">Canal+ said its approach to combating piracy would not change following the acquisition: "Combating piracy remains a strategic priority, and our efforts continue to evolve in line with the changing threat landscape."

(cite index="23-1">Canal+ has also reduced decoder prices for new DStv and GOtv subscribers by up to 40% as part of a broader strategy to revive Africa's biggest pay-TV operator and attract more customers. The move comes as MultiChoice returns to profitability following years of subscriber losses. This is the right instinct. Lower barriers to legal access reduce the incentive to find illegal alternatives. The decoder price reduction is more effective as an anti-piracy measure than a raid.

But decoder prices are not the only barrier. The monthly subscription cost, the content fragmentation, and the perception that DStv is extracting maximum value from a captive market have all contributed to the piracy problem over years. Forensic watermarks cannot fix any of those things.

The pattern, globally: Every major piracy surge follows the same trigger — a legal option that is too expensive, too fragmented, or too restricted. Netflix's rise killed torrent traffic for half a decade because it was cheaper and more convenient than piracy. Streaming fragmentation brought piracy back. DStv's best anti-piracy tool is a good product at a fair price, not TraceMark. Both matter. Only one addresses the root cause.

What this means for South African consumers

// Chapter 04 — The practical picture

For the person currently using an illegal IPTV service: the risk is real and increasing. (cite index="19-1">Individuals face serious charges including money laundering, copyright infringement, and cybercrime offences under the Cybercrimes Act. The management panel infiltration approach means your details can be identified and deactivated without warning. The 819 accounts deactivated in Cape Town in March 2026 belonged to real people who thought they were anonymous.

For the person considering their legal options: the honest picture is that the legal streaming landscape in South Africa is still fragmented and still expensive relative to median income. The streaming fatigue article published here earlier this year covers the build-it-yourself alternative for those with developer skills. For everyone else, the best options remain picking the one or two platforms that have the content you actually watch — and accepting that you will not have everything.

For Canal+ and MultiChoice: the technology is doing what technology can do. The business model question — whether the content, pricing, and packaging are genuinely competitive with the alternatives — is the one that will determine whether the enforcement effort produces lasting results or simply pushes the piracy ecosystem to adapt and return.

The watermarks are clever. The French court ruling is significant. The raids are necessary. And none of it changes the fact that (cite index="18-1">Canal+ is simultaneously the company fighting piracy and the company that industry voices say is actively driving DStv subscribers toward it. That contradiction is the real story.
